newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian economy fairly healthy - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian economy fairly healthy - analysts.

text.p: Cambodia's economy is fairly healthy despite recent political upheaval but still relies too heavily on foreign aid, government officials and analysts said on Monday.
"The economy is more or less okay," said Sok Hach, economic adviser to the Ministry of Finance.
But 1997 and 1998 could be "difficult" years because of uncertainty over future foreign assistance to Cambodia, which derives nearly half its budget from aid, Sok Hach added.
Analysts said it was uncertain how long the international community would continue to pour more than $300 million a year into Cambodia.
Diplomats and aid workers told Reuters they were frustrated with continuing tensions between co-Premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen, which have paralysed the government in recent weeks.

The relationship between the two leaders, who formed an uneasy coalition following U.N.-sponsored elections in 1993, has soured since a deadly March 30 grenade attack on a demonstration led by opposition leader and Ranariddh ally, Sam Rainsy.
The relationship sunk to new lows two weeks ago, when Hun Sen supported dissidents who broke from Ranariddh's royalist FUNCINPEC party.

Those problems have dismayed the international community, whose dollars are vital to the economy and to help finance a hefty balance of payments deficit that stood at more than $500 million in 1996, or nearly 16 percent of gross domestic product.

Some international investors have expressed concern over Cambodia's recent instability and said they were reluctant to increase their stake in the nation, which remains scarred from years of civil war.
But analysts said concern over political problems would probably not cause many nations to cut aid in June, when donors will gather in Paris to hammer out an assistance budget for Cambodia.
Still, Finance Minister Keat Chhon has pointed to the need for reform and has sought to increase the tax base and cut government jobs to counter the nation's heavy reliance on aid.
A monthly Finance Ministry report released this week said Cambodia "faces an important balance of payments deficit," and noted the bloated civil service continues to consume the budget.
More positively, the report said gross domestic product was expected to grow by 6.5 percent in 1997 and inflation for January 1997 was steady at 8.4 percent.
